newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil faces crunch vote for civil service reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil faces crunch vote for civil service reform.

text.p: A setback for the Brazilian government's civil service reform bill in Congress Tuesday could turn into outright disaster later Wednesday when the core of the legislation is up for a vote, lawmakers and analysts said.

The Chamber of Deputies was due to vote in the late afternoon or evening on an opposition amendment which would keep the life-time job guarantees for civil servants, the most important aspect of the civil service reform initiative.

"If we lose tonight, that's it. The government will have to scrap civil service reform altogether," said Roberto Brant, a member of the Chamber of Deputies close to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.

The president suffered a latest setback to his struggling reform program Tuesday when the government failed to defeat an opposition amendment striking down one of the most important articles of the civil service reform bill.
The bill is considered crucial to Brazil's efforts to reduce spending and narrow its public sector deficit.
The amendment approved Tuesday prevents state and municipal governments from setting their own pay ceilings below a 10,800-real ($10,188) monthly cap for federal workers included in the reform.
The sub-ceiling would have helped cash-strapped states and municipalities to reduce spending on payrolls which accounts for most or in some cases all their revenues.
"The real losers are the country as a whole and the states because they will not be able to cut spending on pay as they had hoped," said presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral.
Government whips blamed the defeat on a low turnout among lawmakers and said Wednesday's vote on the issue of job stability would be better attended.

Left-wing opposition lawmakers, revelling in the government's difficulties, said the result showed Cardoso no longer flexed the political muscle to get the three-fifths majorities in Congress needed for constitutional reform.
"The government hasn't got a hope of approving job stability tonight," said Workers Party deputy Marcelo Deda. "If it lost the warm-up last night, how will it win the big match?"

Tuesday's defeat was also a blow to Luis Eduardo Magalhaes who was appointed chief whip in the lower house last week amid high hopes that he could turn around the government's fortunes in an increasingly unmanageable Chamber of Deputies.
"It's clear the government cannot count on its majority in the lower house," said Maria Tereza Sedek, a political analyst with the Sao Paulo-based thinktank IDESP.
